source_title: Meet Landon Hoberman: Teen’s campaign prevents 8.1 million plastic utensils
source_excerpt: Landon Hoberman is just 17, from New Jersey, but heâs demonstrating how one small change in the way we eat at restaurants can make a big difference for the environment. He has been lauded for his campaign to get restaurants to stop automatically including plastic cutlery with takeaway and delivery orders, which has stopped 8.1 million pieces of single-use cutlery from going to landfill. The effort has also saved participating restaurants more than $200,000, proving that cutting waste can be good for the planet and local businesses. Hobermanâs work has earned national recognition as a 2026 Barron Prize winner, an award that honours young people who have made meaningful contributions to their communities and the environment, as per the award's website. His idea did not require a complicated invention or an expensive new technology. Instead, it focused on changing a default habit: asking customers whether they actually need plastic forks, knives, and spoons before restaurants include them with an order. Read more about his idea here, as per Barron Prize website:A simple question with a big impactEvery day, restaurants across the country place plastic cutlery into takeout bags and delivery orders, often without asking whether customers want or need it. Many people eating at home already have reusable utensils, while others may not use the plastic items at all. Once discarded, those utensils add to the enormous amount of single-use plastic that ends up in landfills, waterways, and natural environments.Hobermanâs campaign challenged that routine by encouraging restaurants to make cutlery optional rather than automatic. Instead of placing utensils in every order, participating businesses could ask customers to request them or offer a simple opt in choice at checkout. That small shift means plastic is only used when it is genuinely needed, reducing waste without making customers give up convenience.The results have been incredible. The campaign has kept 8.1 million single-use utensils out of circulation, preventing a lot of plastic from being manufactured, circulated, used once and discarded. The environmental benefit is significant, but the financial benefit matters too. Restaurants have saved more than $200,000 by avoiding the cost of purchasing and packaging utensils that many customers never use.Recognition from the Barron PrizeHoberman is among the young people honored by the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which celebrates young leaders across the United States and Canada. The 2026 winners include students working on environmental protection, accessibility, health care, food recovery, and social justice. The Barron Prize highlights projects that begin with a personal concern and grow into practical action that benefits others.His project is simple but impactful as it deals with a problem that most people go through every day but hardly ever question. Plastic utensils are easy to overlook because they appear quietly in a takeout bag or delivery box. By drawing attention to that practice, Hoberman transformed a trivial annoyance into a measurable crusade: Millions of utensils not used, hundreds of thousands of dollars saved.The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection has also recognised Hoberman among its award winners, reflecting the value of his work at both the local and statewide level. Recognition from environmental organizations helps bring attention to the idea that waste reduction does not always require sweeping regulation. Sometimes it begins with a young person asking businesses and consumers to reconsider an automatic choice.Why reducing plastic cutlery mattersSingle-use plastic utensils may seem small compared with bottles, bags, or packaging, but their collective impact is enormous. They are used for only a few minutes but can linger in the environment for centuries.They are lightweight and often too small or contaminated to be easily recycled, which means that many of them end up in landfills or become litter, harming wildlife and polluting waterways.Reducing unnecessary utensils also lowers the hidden environmental costs of production. Making plastic cutlery requires fossil fuels, manufacturing energy, transportation, and packaging. When millions of utensils are avoided, those upstream impacts are reduced as well. Hobermanâs campaign therefore addresses pollution at its source rather than simply cleaning it up after the fact.The financial savings add another persuasive argument for restaurants. Cutlery, napkins, condiment packets, and other extras may appear inexpensive individually, but across thousands of orders they become a meaningful expense. By giving customers the choice, restaurants can reduce purchasing costs, cut packaging waste, and still provide utensils to people who need them.A model other communities can followWhat makes Hobermanâs campaign especially powerful is that it can be replicated almost anywhere. Restaurants, delivery apps, schools, offices, and event organizers can all adopt a simple policy of providing utensils only on request. The change does not require banning plastic outright or asking customers to carry their own cutlery everywhere. It simply asks whether the item is needed before it is included.His success also demonstrates the power of youth when they find a practical solution and continue to promote it. Instead of waiting for adults or policymakers to act, Hoberman built a campaign around one, attainable goal. The result is a model that other students, environmental groups, and business owners can learn from.Already 17-year-old Landon Hoberman has diverted millions of pieces of plastic from the waste stream and saved restaurants more than $200,000.His story is a reminder of how meaningful change to our environment can start with something as ordinary as a plastic fork, and how a single thoughtful question can lead to results in the millions.You use AI every day.
